opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things that sounds like a boring implementation detail but actually matters a lot for how well the model performs.

There are basically a few families of approaches. The simplest is just rewriting the whole file. The model outputs the full new contents, and that's very robust in the sense that there's no ambiguity about what the result should be. But it's expensive and slow for large files, and you get this subtle failure mode where the model gets lazy and writes things like "rest of the code unchanged" in a comment, and suddenly you've deleted half the file.

Then there are diff formats, like unified diffs with line numbers. Those look attractive because they're compact and they're a standard format. In practice, models are pretty bad at line numbers. Counting is hard for them, and if the file has changed during the session, the numbers drift. So you get patches that don't apply cleanly, or worse, apply in the wrong place.

What we found worked really well is a string-replace style edit: the model gives an old string and a new string, and the old string has to match exactly once in the file. The nice properties there are that the model doesn't have to count anything. It just quotes the code it's looking at, which models are very good at. And the uniqueness requirement gives you a natural error signal. If the string isn't found, or it appears multiple times, you return an error and the model can just include more surrounding context and try again. Failing loudly is much better than failing silently.

The general principle I'd take away is to think about the tool from the model's perspective. Put yourself in its shoes. If you were a smart person who could only see the text and had to specify an edit without an IDE, what format would you get right on the first try? Pick formats that resemble what the model has seen a lot of naturally, avoid things that require precise bookkeeping, and make sure that mistakes surface as clear, actionable errors rather than corrupting the file.

We actually spent a surprising amount of time on the tool interface compared to the prompt itself. Things like making paths absolute instead of relative removed a whole class of errors. A lot of agent performance comes down to this kind of ergonomic work on the tools.

r001.rationale: The response says string-replace edits “worked really well,” then explains why they outperform diffs: no line counting and clear errors when a match is missing or ambiguous.

r002.rationale: It describes full-file rewriting as robust and unambiguous, but does not identify it as the most accurate method among those tested.

r003.rationale: It says full-file rewriting is expensive and slow for large files because the model must output the full new contents, conveying the cost of the additional output.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things that sounds like a boring implementation detail and ends up being one of the biggest levers on whether an agent actually works.

The way I think about it, there's a spectrum. On one end you have the model just rewriting the whole file. That's the simplest possible interface, it's basically impossible to get malformed, and the model is really good at it because it's just generating code. The problem is cost and latency. If you've got a two-thousand-line file and you want to change one line, you're paying to regenerate two thousand lines, and you're also opening yourself up to the model getting lazy in the middle and dropping a function, or writing "rest of file unchanged" as a comment, which is a real failure mode we saw a lot.

On the other end you have diffs. Unified diffs are very compact, but the model has to get line numbers and context lines exactly right, and models are honestly not great at counting lines. You end up with a lot of patches that don't apply, and then you need some fuzzy matching layer that tries to rescue them, and now you've got a system where the model thinks an edit succeeded when it actually landed somewhere slightly wrong. That's the worst outcome, because the model's picture of the file drifts from reality.

The thing we converged on in Claude Code is search and replace. The model gives you the old string and the new string. That's nice because it doesn't require any line arithmetic, it's robust to the file having shifted around since the model last read it, and it's trivial to validate. If the old string doesn't appear exactly once, you just fail loudly and the model tries again with more context. Models are very good at copying text verbatim, much better than they are at counting, so you're playing to their strengths.

There are tradeoffs there too. If the model wants to change something that appears many times, it has to include enough surrounding context to disambiguate, and sometimes it gets whitespace or indentation subtly wrong and the match fails. But a failed match is a recoverable error, and the model learns pretty quickly to just read the file again and retry. We'd rather have errors that are loud and cheap than silent corruptions.

The other thing I'd say is that the right answer depends on the model. Early on we did a lot of hand-holding, formats that were very tolerant, lots of fuzzy matching. As the models got better at tool use, we could move to stricter, simpler formats, and the simpler format actually made the model more reliable, because there was less ambiguity about what a correct call looked like. So my general advice is: pick the format that's easiest to validate and easiest for the model to copy, make failures visible, and don't be afraid to revisit the choice as the models improve. The format that was right a year ago is probably not the right one today.

r001.rationale: The response says search and replace is the method they converged on and explains that models copy text reliably, supporting it as the most reliable approach.

r002.rationale: It describes full-file rewriting as simple and says the model is good at it, but does not identify it as the most accurate method; it also notes that rewriting can drop functions.

r003.rationale: It explains that changing one line in a 2,000-line file requires regenerating all 2,000 lines, making the method costly.

astra-6.text:
I think the main tradeoff is between how easy the edit is for the model to express and how reliably you can apply it. You can ask the model to rewrite the whole file, which is a very simple interface. But if it’s changing three lines in a thousand-line file, you’re spending a lot of output tokens copying unchanged code, and you create opportunities for accidental changes elsewhere.

At the other end, you can ask for a very precise diff. That’s much more efficient, but now the model has to get the patch format and the location right. Line numbers are particularly awkward because they can shift as edits happen.

Search-and-replace is a useful middle ground: the model gives you a chunk of existing text and the replacement. It doesn’t need to count lines, and it only outputs the relevant portion of the file. But the old text has to match, and it needs enough context to identify the right occurrence. If the same snippet appears in five places, you don’t want to silently pick one.

So I’d assess the whole loop, not just the representation: how often does an edit apply correctly, how much does it cost, and what happens when it fails? A tool that clearly reports an ambiguous match and lets the model retry can be more useful than one that tries to guess what the model meant.

r001.rationale: It describes search-and-replace as a useful middle ground but does not identify it as the most reliable method Erik found.

r002.rationale: It calls rewriting the whole file simple and notes risks, but does not identify it as the most accurate method tested.

r003.rationale: It notes that rewriting large files uses many tokens, but does not clearly say the token requirements can make the method cost-prohibitive.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s a tradeoff between making the edit easy for the model to express and making it reliable to apply. The simplest approach is to have it rewrite the whole file. That’s pretty unambiguous, but if you’re changing three lines in a thousand-line file, you spend a lot of tokens copying unchanged code, and you create opportunities for accidental changes.

At the other end, you can ask for a diff. That’s much more compact, but you’re asking the model to get a fairly precise format right. Line numbers and hunk lengths are extra bookkeeping that doesn’t really contribute to the change you want.

A nice middle ground is search-and-replace: give me the exact block of existing code, and then the block that should replace it. You avoid reproducing the whole file, and you don’t need line numbers. But the search block has to match, and it needs enough context to identify a unique location.

So I’d evaluate the whole loop: how often does the model express the right change, how often can your tool apply it, and how well can it recover when something fails? A compact edit format isn’t necessarily cheaper if it takes three retries to get it applied.

r001.rationale: The response describes search-and-replace as a “nice middle ground,” but does not identify it as the most reliable method or attribute that finding to Erik Schluntz.

r002.rationale: It calls whole-file rewriting “pretty unambiguous,” but does not say it was the most accurate method among those tested.

r003.rationale: It says large-file edits spend many tokens copying unchanged code, but does not communicate that the token requirements can make full-file regeneration cost-prohibitive.
